chapters.name: Chapter 1: Finding the right AI opportunity

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What AI does well in business today
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the kinds of business work today's AI tools handle well and poorly.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of business tasks, you will identify which ones today's AI tools handle well and which need a person to check or decide, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Most business AI today is generative AI: tools like ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini that write, summarize, sort and answer in plain language. Other AI is built into software you may already use, such as email filters, sales forecasts and fraud alerts.
AI is strong at first drafts (emails, posts, proposals), summaries (meetings, long documents, reviews), sorting and tagging (customer questions, receipts), brainstorming, and answering common questions from your own information.
AI is weak at exact facts it was not given, final decisions about people or money, anything needing a license (legal, medical, tax advice), and situations where a mistake is costly and hard to catch. In those, a person must check or decide.
Words to know:
- Generative AI: AI that creates text, images or other content from a request.
- Use case: a specific job a tool is used for.
Try it now: List five tasks in a business or organization you know. Mark each one "AI strong", "AI with checking" or "keep for people", with one reason.
You can now tell which business tasks AI handles well and which need a person.

check.q: Which task is today's AI weak at?
options: Giving final tax advice for your business
check.why: Anything needing a license, like tax advice, needs a person or a professional.

check.q: Your shop gets hundreds of online reviews. How could AI help first?
options: Summarize them to find the most common complaints
Reply to angry customers with no one checking
Decide which staff to let go based on reviews
check.why: Summarizing many reviews is a strength of AI, and a person still decides what to do.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Mapping where time goes
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Map an organization's repeated tasks and spot the best AI candidates.
This lesson builds toward: For a real or practice organization, you will list the repeated tasks in a normal week and calculate the hours each one takes, with the top five tasks by hours circled.
The best AI opportunities hide in repeated, time-consuming work. Walk through a normal week and list tasks by department or role: sales, customer service, marketing, admin, finance, operations.
For each task, estimate how often it happens and how long it takes. A task done 20 times a week for 10 minutes is over three hours a week. That is where AI pays off.
Look for patterns: answering the same questions, writing similar emails, copying information between places, summarizing notes, building schedules. These are classic AI or automation candidates.
Step by step:
- List the tasks done in a normal week, by role.
- Estimate how often and how long for each.
- Multiply to get hours per week.
- Circle the top five by hours.
- Mark which of those fit AI's strengths.
Words to know:
- Repetitive task: work done the same way again and again.
- Time audit: a list of tasks and how much time each takes.
Try it now: Do a time audit for one role in a real or practice organization. List at least eight tasks with hours per week, and circle the top three AI candidates.
You can now map an organization's repeated work and spot the best AI candidates.

check.q: A task happens 12 times a week and takes 15 minutes each time. How many hours a week is that?
check.why: 12 times 15 minutes is 180 minutes, which is 3 hours.

check.q: You are mapping time at a nonprofit. Which task do you look at first for AI?
options: Writing the same thank-you email to donors every week
check.why: Repeated, similar writing tasks are where AI pays off most.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Scoring opportunities for value and risk
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Score AI ideas on value, effort and risk and pick one to pursue.
This lesson builds toward: Given your top AI candidates, you will score each one on value, effort and risk and choose one to pursue first, noting any private data involved.
Not every AI idea is worth doing first. Score each candidate from 1 to 5 on three things. Value: how much time, money or customer happiness it adds. Effort: how hard it is to set up and learn. Risk: what happens if the AI gets it wrong, and whether private data is involved.
Pick a quick win: high value, low effort, low risk. Drafting replies to common customer emails, with a person reviewing them, is a classic quick win. Using AI to decide who gets hired or approved for help is high risk and not a first project.
Check data and privacy early. If the task uses customer, employee, donor or health information, find out what your AI tool does with the data and whether a business version with stronger privacy is needed.
Step by step:
- List your top three candidates.
- Score each 1-5 on value, effort and risk.
- Prefer high value, low effort, low risk.
- Note any private data involved.
- Choose one to pursue first.
Words to know:
- Quick win: a project that gives clear value fast with little effort and risk.
- Risk: the chance and cost of something going wrong.
Try it now: Score your top three AI candidates for value, effort and risk in a small table. Choose one quick win and write two sentences on why.
You can now score AI ideas for value, effort and risk and pick a smart first project.

check.q: When you score an AI idea, what does "effort" mean?
options: How hard it is to set up and learn
check.why: Effort is how hard the idea is to set up and learn.

check.q: Two ideas have the same value. One uses health records and one uses public product facts. Which do you pick first?
options: The health records idea, because it is harder
The product facts idea, because it has lower risk
check.why: With equal value, choose the lower-risk idea that does not involve private data.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Making the case and proving it

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing a one-page AI business case
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page business case that a boss, board or partner can say yes to.
This lesson builds toward: For the task you chose, you will write a one-page AI business case, with all six parts and real numbers from your time audit.
A business case explains why a project is worth doing. Keep it to one page so busy people read it.
Include six parts: the problem (in hours or dollars), the proposed AI solution and tool, the expected benefit, the cost (subscriptions, training time), the risks and how you will control them, and how you will measure success.
Use real numbers from your time audit. "Staff spend 4 hours a week answering the same 10 questions. An AI-drafted reply library, checked by staff, could cut that to 1.5 hours, saving about 10 hours a month." AI can help you draft the page; you supply the facts.
Step by step:
- Problem: what it costs now in time or money.
- Solution: the AI tool and how it will be used.
- Benefit: expected savings or improvement.
- Cost: money and training time.
- Risks and controls: who checks the AI's work.
- Success measure: the number you will track.
Words to know:
- Business case: a short document explaining why a project is worth doing.
- Control: a step that reduces risk, like a person reviewing AI output.
Try it now: Write a one-page business case for your chosen quick win with all six parts. You may ask AI to tidy the wording, but check every number.
You can now write a short, numbers-based business case for an AI project.

check.q: Which part of a business case says who checks the AI's work?
check.why: Risks and controls say what could go wrong and who checks the AI's output.

check.q: Your boss asks why the AI project is worth it. What makes your case strongest?
options: A long report with no numbers
A list of every AI tool you found
Real numbers from your time audit showing hours saved
check.why: Real numbers from your own time audit show the expected benefit clearly.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Running a small pilot
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan and run a two-week AI pilot with clear rules and a before-and-after measure.
This lesson builds toward: For a small AI pilot, you will plan and run the pilot with a baseline, clear rules and a daily log, recording the same numbers before and after.
A pilot is a small, time-limited test. It lets you learn cheaply before spending more. Two weeks with one or two people is often enough.
Measure before you start. Track the current numbers for a few days: time spent, number of tasks, errors or customer complaints. Then run the pilot and track the same numbers.
Set clear rules: which tasks use AI, who checks the output, what information must never go into the tool (customer, employee or donor private details, passwords, bank numbers), and what to do if the AI gets something wrong.
Step by step:
- Pick one or two people and a two-week window.
- Record the baseline numbers for a few days.
- Write simple rules: tasks, who checks, what never goes in.
- Run the pilot and keep a short daily log.
- Record the same numbers at the end.
Words to know:
- Pilot: a small, time-limited test of a new idea.
- Baseline: the numbers before a change, used to compare after.
Try it now: Write a pilot plan for your quick win: people, dates, baseline numbers, rules and the daily log format. If you can, run a one-day practice version and record the numbers.
You can now plan and run a small AI pilot with rules and before-and-after numbers.

check.q: How long is a typical small AI pilot in this course?
check.why: Two weeks with one or two people is often enough to learn cheaply.

check.q: You are about to start a pilot tomorrow. What must you do first?
options: Record baseline numbers for a few days
Give the tool every customer's details
Tell staff to stop checking AI output
check.why: A baseline lets you compare before and after.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Measuring results and deciding what is next
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare pilot results to the baseline and recommend expand, change or stop.
This lesson builds toward: Given your baseline and pilot numbers, you will compare the results and recommend expand, change or stop, counting time spent fixing AI mistakes, in three sentences.
At the end of the pilot, compare. Did time go down? Did quality hold or improve? Did customers or staff notice? Numbers matter, but also ask the people who used it what helped and what got in the way.
Watch for hidden costs: time spent fixing AI mistakes, staff confusion, or customers who disliked the change. A tool that saves 3 hours but causes 2 hours of fixes saves only 1.
Make a clear recommendation. Expand if it worked. Change if it partly worked. Stop if it did not, and say what you learned. Stopping a pilot is not failure; it saved you from a bigger mistake.
Step by step:
- Put baseline and pilot numbers side by side.
- Subtract time spent fixing AI mistakes.
- Ask the people who used it two questions: what helped, what got in the way.
- Recommend expand, change or stop, in three sentences.
Words to know:
- Hidden cost: a cost that is easy to miss, like time spent fixing mistakes.
- Recommendation: your advice on what to do next, with reasons.
Try it now: Final task: put your before-and-after numbers in a table (real or from your practice day), subtract hidden costs, and write a three-sentence recommendation to go with your one-page business case.
You can now find, justify, test and judge an AI project in a business or organization.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Task and tool The task is high risk, like hiring decisions, or no tool is named. A repeated, lower-risk task and a named AI tool, with any private data noted. Shows the value, effort and risk scores that led to this choice. Business case Missing parts, or no numbers. One page with the problem, solution, benefit, cost, risks and controls, and a success measure. Every number comes from the time audit and is easy to check. Time savings estimate The savings are a guess with no time audit. Savings are based on how often the task happens and how long it takes. Also estimates time needed to check the AI's work. Pilot and baseline No baseline, or the pilot had no rules. Baseline and end numbers recorded, with rules on tasks, who checks and what never goes in. A daily log shows what worked and what went wrong. Recommendation No clear recommendation, or it ignores the numbers. Three sentences recommending expand, change or stop, based on before-and-after numbers. Subtracts time spent fixing AI mistakes and includes what users said. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why ask the people who used the AI tool what got in the way?
options: To find problems the numbers might not show
check.why: Users can name hidden costs and problems that numbers miss.

check.q: The pilot saved time but customers complained about the new replies. What do you recommend?
options: Expand it to everyone right away
Change it, such as adding a staff review step, and test again
check.why: If it partly worked, change it and test again.
